question: Did the Prophet ﷺ see Allah?
asked: Someone heard in a lecture in Urdu that the Prophet ﷺ saw Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. Is this true or not?
answer:
The answer to this has multiple parts. First and foremost, this is the issue of ru'yah, or seeing Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala, and it is one of the key fundamentals of Sunni theology. In contrast, non-Sunnis, the Mu'tazila and the Twelver Shia and others, don't have this perspective. Ahl al-Sunnah say that the belief is that we will see Allah 'azza wa jall in the hereafter, and this is something that we say is affirmed in the Qur'an and in the Sunnah.

As for the Qur'an, there are at least four verses, two of which are explicit and two of which are implicit, about the issue of seeing Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. As for the explicit ones, of them is the one I just recited in Salat al-Isha: "On that day, faces will be nadirah" (nadirah means to be brightened) "because they will be looking at their Lord." So this is an explicit ayah of the Qur'an. On the Day of Judgment, the faces of the believers will be bright, shining, happy, because they will be looking at Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala.

And there is another verse that is also explicit, where Allah says in the Qur'an that the people who reject Allah, the kafir, on that day there shall be a barrier between them and Allah: mahjub, hijab. Imam al-Shafi'i said: when the kafir has a barrier between him and Allah, this implies the Muslim has no barrier between him and Allah on Judgment Day. So he derived this from the verse: why would Allah 'azza wa jall punish them, why will there be a hijab? This means those who believe in Allah, there will not be that.

And from the ahadith, they are mutawatir. There are more than 15 narrations from the Prophet ﷺ, reported in every book of hadith: Bukhari, Muslim, every one of them. And of the most explicit ones, and it is in Sahih Bukhari, the Prophet ﷺ said, "You will see your Lord with your eyes," on Judgment Day. And in the famous hadith of Abu Hurayrah (this is Bukhari and Muslim), the Prophet ﷺ was walking with the Sahabah, and there was the full moon outside, and he said, "You will verily see your Lord the way that you are seeing this moon." The comparison is not, a'udhu billah, between the moon and Allah. The comparison is between how the people see the moon and how the people will see Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala.

And he then clarified, and he said, "You will not be pushing one another to see Him." You will not be arguing or having a problem. When the moon is full, everybody is equal; they can see the moon. It's not as if some celebrity comes and you cannot see. No, it's not like that. Allah 'azza wa jall will be visible to all the believers. Nobody's going to be fighting or anything like this. So you will not be cramping one another to see Him: la tudammun. In another riwayah, la tudarrun: you will not be harming one another to see Him. So this is explicit that there is belief in seeing Him in the hereafter.

Now, the other groups, they deny this. And they say Allah says in the Qur'an, "Eyes cannot encompass Him, and He encompasses everyone's eyes": la tudrikuhu al-absar. And they say Allah said to Musa, "You will never see Me." So they use this Qur'anic evidence, and they say we cannot see Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala.

And the response is: Allah 'azza wa jall says, "Eyes cannot encompass." And we are not encompassing; we are simply seeing. Eyes cannot fully grasp Allah. Agreed, even in the akhirah. But there is no negation of simply seeing Allah. Idrak is not the same as ru'yah; idrak is a higher level. And when Allah says la tudrikuhu al-absar, it is true: eyes cannot fully comprehend Allah. They cannot encompass Allah.

As for the verse of Musa, in fact, we flip it around, and we say: the very fact that Musa said,

> قَالَ رَبِّ أَرِنِي أَنظُرْ إِلَيْكَ

signifies that Musa knew that it is possible to see Allah. And Musa assumed: since I have been chosen to speak to Allah, now I want to also be chosen to see Allah. The very fact that Musa asks indicates it is in the realm of possibility. It is not befitting that Musa asks the impossible. Musa 'alayhi al-salam knew that people will see Allah. He wanted to expedite; he said, in this world let me see. So Allah said, "You will not see Me," meaning in this world you cannot see Me. This is how Ahl al-Sunnah interpret this.

Now, as for the Prophet ﷺ in particular seeing Allah, this was a controversy that occurred in the time of the Sahabah. Ibn Abbas and Ubayy and others of the Sahabah, in fact some of them, would swear, "I swear by Allah that the Prophet ﷺ saw Allah when he went on the Isra wal-Mi'raj." So they would give qasam that he saw Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala on the Isra wal-Mi'raj. And they interpreted the verses in Surat al-Najm (if you read it), they interpreted those passages as meaning that the Prophet ﷺ saw Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala.

One of the students of Ibn Abbas came to Aisha, and he said that the Prophet ﷺ saw Allah. And Aisha said, "What did you say?" This hadith is in Bukhari. He repeated what he had heard from his teacher Ibn Abbas. And Aisha famously remarked, "My hair is standing on end from what you have said," meaning I'm shocked from what you have said. "Don't you know that Allah says, la tudrikuhu al-absar wa huwa yudriku al-absar?" So she quoted the same verse. So the man said, "Wait, hold on a sec. Doesn't Allah say in Surat al-Najm...?" So Aisha says (this hadith is in Bukhari), "I was the first person to ask the Prophet about these ayat, and that was Jibreel, not Allah. He saw Jibreel, not Allah." Surat al-Najm is about Jibreel. So if you read Surat al-Najm, now you understand it's about Jibreel. This hadith is in Bukhari.

So there seems to be a conflict: Ibn Abbas says one thing, Aisha says another. Some have said there's no real conflict, because there is one report from Ibn Abbas that he said, "He saw Him with his qalb, bi-qalbihi, he saw Him." And this means that Ibn Abbas is saying that the seeing was not the type of seeing that we understand; it was a different, metaphysical type. So some have said there's no conflict, and some have said there are two opinions, and Allah 'azza wa jall knows best.

Imam al-Nawawi remarks in his commentary on Sahih Muslim, Imam al-Nawawi says, that the correct opinion, and the majority of the scholars' opinion, is that the Prophet ﷺ saw Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala in the positive: he saw Allah. This is Nawawi's interpretation. Others commented, including Imam Ibn Taymiyyah and others, and they said no, this is not the majority opinion; this is Nawawi's assumption that it is the majority opinion. And in fact, they argue the majority opinion is that of Aisha: that he did not see Allah.

And they quote many evidences. Of them, the same hadith of the moon. The Prophet ﷺ is speaking in the future, it's in the future: "You shall" (the sin in Arabic means for the future) "you shall see your Lord." So he didn't say, "Oh, you know, I saw Him and you guys are going to see Him." No.

And also the famous hadith of Dajjal (we mentioned it many times when we talked about Dajjal), that the Prophet ﷺ said: you will see the Dajjal, he will claim to be your Lord, and know that you will not see your Lord in this world. This is an explicit hadith. But there is a clause, fi al-dunya, which means what? You will see Him in the akhirah. So explicitly the Prophet ﷺ is saying: anybody who claims to be God, he is not God, and the Dajjal is claiming to be God. So he is saying, don't be fooled, you shall not see your Lord in this world. So the fact that he said this, and he's the one saying it, means he did not see Allah 'azza wa jall in this world as well.

Also, there are other evidences as well. Of them is the famous hadith of Abu Dharr al-Ghifari. Now, Imam al-Nawawi has a different interpretation. It is in Sahih Muslim, and it is an authentic hadith in Sahih Muslim. Abu Dharr al-Ghifari asked the Prophet ﷺ, "Ya Rasulallah, hal ra'ayta rabbak?" You cannot get more explicit than this: "Did you see your Lord?" in the Isra wal-Mi'raj. And the Prophet ﷺ responded, "Nurun, anna arah": "There was light; how could I see Him?" Now, the majority of scholars say "there was light, how could I see Him" means that he saw the hijab of Allah, which was made out of light: hijabuhu al-nur, and that hadith is also in Muslim. And the other interpretation is that he didn't negate seeing Him; he's asking a rhetorical question, and that's not the same as saying "I didn't see Him." And they have their interpretation. Allah knows best.

It appears that Aisha... And by the way, between Aisha and Ibn Abbas, Aisha is senior, and Aisha is the more knowledgeable, and Aisha is the one who accompanied the Prophet for much more. Ibn Abbas, how old was he when the Prophet passed away? Who can tell me? Twelve or thirteen years old. Aisha and Ibn Abbas are not the same. Aisha accompanied the Prophet for all of Madinah, and she lived with the Prophet. Ibn Abbas is a nephew, and he is the great scholar, but he doesn't compare with Aisha. So Aisha is saying, "I asked about these verses; that's not correct." So Ibn Abbas had an interpretation, and Allah 'azza wa jall knows best.

Now, this is with regards to seeing in the Isra wal-Mi'raj. There is another controversy about the Prophet ﷺ seeing Allah, and this is based on a hadith that is reported by five Sahabah. It is reported in Tirmidhi and Musnad Ahmad and a number of books, and it is authentic. There are many Sahabah that reported this. In fact, Tirmidhi narrates it, and he said, "I asked Imam al-Bukhari about this hadith." Tirmidhi was Bukhari's main student; actually, Muslim was his main student, and Tirmidhi was his second main student. So Muslim and Tirmidhi are Bukhari's two main students. And Tirmidhi wrote his book while Bukhari was alive. And so in Sunan al-Tirmidhi, Jami' al-Tirmidhi, he said, "I asked Imam al-Bukhari about this hadith," which one I'm going to narrate to you, and Imam al-Bukhari said, "Hadha hadithun sahih": it is an authentic hadith. So we have an authentic hadith.

What does the hadith say? This hadith says, in one version of the hadith, that we prayed Fajr, and the Prophet ﷺ was delayed in coming out. We waited for him. We prayed Fajr. He said, "Stay where you are; I have something to tell you." Then the hadith goes: "My Lord came to me in the best image in my sleep. In the best image He came to me, in my sleep." And I'm quoting you the hadith; you can look this up. "And He placed His hand between my shoulders, on my chest, until I could feel the coolness on my chest. And He said, 'Ya Muhammad.' I said, 'Labbayka wa sa'dayk'" (meaning I'm answering Your call, O Allah). "He said, 'Fima yakhtasimu al-mala' al-a'la?' Do you know what the highest of the angels are arguing over?"

The hadith is very long; it goes on and on. He said, "I don't know," this and that. Then Allah 'azza wa jall gave him that response, after the hand was placed. And then the Prophet ﷺ said, "Everything became clear to me, and I said: they are arguing over the darajat and the kaffarat." The darajat: they're arguing what good deed is the most precious and blessed to Allah, that will raise you to the highest ranks. And what good deed is the one that forgives most of the sins. This is the argument of the angels. They're not arguing who has more money, who has the bigger house, who has the bigger car. All of this is irrelevant. What are the angels arguing about? What deed is the most pleasing to Allah that will raise you high, and what deed will forgive the most sins.

So he was asked, what are they? So the Prophet ﷺ said: as for the darajat, perfecting wudu when it's difficult (it's cold, and you do the wudu properly), and in the masjid, waiting for the next salah to come. This is them. And as for the kaffarat:

> فَإِطْعَامُ الطَّعَامِ وَإِفْشَاءُ السَّلَامِ وَطِيبُ الْكَلَامِ وَالصَّلَاةُ وَالنَّاسُ نِيَامٌ

So he gave the kaffarat. Then the hadith goes on; it's a long hadith. This hadith is very explicit: ra'aytu rabbi fi ahsani surah. But it says fi manami, in my sleep. So based on this, the majority of scholars said for the Prophet ﷺ to see Allah in his sleep is ja'iz, because sleep is not the same as being awake, and a dream is not the same as reality. So whatever he saw, it was a dream that was true, because all the dreams of the prophets are true. And it is permissible for the prophets to see Allah in a dream, but not in real life, because a dream is not the same as real life. Is that clear?

Now, the question that arises from all of this, before we move on to the last one. Jayyid: **we acknowledge the Prophet ﷺ saw Allah in a dream. He did not see Allah in a wakeful state; he did not see Allah in the Isra wal-Mi'raj. And the believers will see Allah in the hereafter.** Now, can anyone else see Allah in a dream?

And the response is: there is no evidence to suggest this, and it is not befitting for anyone other than the Prophet ﷺ. And there's a famous story narrated from Abdul Qadir al-Jilani, the famous shaykh, the famous zahid and 'abid and muttaqi imam, the famous scholar and the famous ascetic and worshipper, Abdul Qadir al-Jilani: that one day he fell asleep, and he saw a big light in the dream, and the light said to him, "I am Allah, and I have chosen you, and you are my preferred of my 'ibad and my awliya'," and this and that, "and you no longer have to do the salawat and the wudu and the zakat. Taklif is now lifted from you."

Abdul Qadir al-Jilani told his students, when they narrated to us, that he said to this entity, "You are not Allah. You are shaytan. You are shaytan." So the entity said, "How do you know? I mean, I'm a bright light. How do you know?" And Abdul Qadir al-Jilani said, "Taklif was not lifted from even the prophets. How can it be lifted from me? Even the prophets had to worship Allah. How can anybody come and say to me I don't have to worship Allah? You must be a Dajjal or a shaytan or something." And so he woke up, and it was indeed obvious what he had seen.

So in any case, there is no evidence to suggest that anyone other than the prophets can see Allah in a dream, and even the prophets do not see Allah in a wakeful state.
